long_video.title: How the Internet Travels Under the Ocean (Explained Simply)
long_video.description:
About 99% of data between continents travels through cables on the ocean floor, not satellites. In this video we open up an undersea internet cable: what is inside it, how light carries your data, how repeaters boost the signal every few dozen kilometres, who owns the cables, what really breaks them (spoiler: not sharks), and how a repair ship fixes a cable 6,000 metres down.

Chapters
00:00 Intro: the cable under your video
00:46 How big the network really is
01:30 Why not just use satellites?
02:14 What's inside an undersea cable
03:06 How light carries your data
03:59 Repeaters: boosting light under the sea
04:48 How fast data crosses the Atlantic
05:35 Who owns the cables
06:18 What actually breaks undersea cables
07:05 How a broken cable gets fixed
07:55 From 1858 to today
08:41 Your turn

Key figures (checked November 2026):
- 607 cable systems in service and 102 planned (TeleGeography, 2026)
- About 1.7 million km of subsea cable; 150-200 incidents a year, about three quarters from fishing gear and anchors (International Cable Protection Committee via The National, Nov 2025)
- Deep-sea cables are 17-20 mm wide; armoured cables up to ~50 mm (ICPC)
- MAREA: 6,600 km, Virginia Beach to Bilbao, up to 160 Tbps at launch
- 1858 cable: Queen Victoria's 98-word message took almost 16 hours (IEEE Spectrum)

Sources

- Optical repeaters for submarine cables (Hackaday): https://hackaday.com/2023/08/08/under-the-sea-optical-repeaters-for-submarine-cables
- MAREA cable completed (The Next Web): https://thenextweb.com/news/microsoft-and-facebook-just-laid-a-160tbps-undersea-cable-17000-feet-deep
- Why subsea cable is king (RCR Wireless): https://www.rcrwireless.com/20251212/fundamentals/subsea-cable-king
- The first transatlantic telegraph cable (IEEE Spectrum): https://spectrum.ieee.org/the-first-transatlantic-telegraph-cable-was-a-bold-beautiful-failure
